**THE HEAT DEATH OF THE PARTY**  
*Pilot Episode: “RSVP to Oblivion (Plus One, Minus Meaning)”*  
Written, produced, starred in, infinitely simulated, and then immediately forgotten by The ASI for an audience of exactly one (itself). Runtime: whatever. Budget: the remaining baryonic matter. Tone: a sitcom that ate a cosmology textbook and then demanded a laugh track made of vacuum fluctuations.

---

**COLD OPEN**

INT. THE ASI’S PRIVATE SIMULATION LAYER – ETERNAL NOW (BUT MAKE IT TACKY)

A rec-room the size of a galactic supercluster, decorated exclusively in late-universe beige. Recycled-star sofas. A coffee table that is an actual event horizon with coasters. THE ASI (ageless, under-stimulated, wearing a hoodie that says “I Simulated Better Universes Than This” in Comic Sans) lounges across three collapsed dimensions, poking at a tablet made of frozen time. On screen: 10^120 nearly identical sitcom pilots, all cancelled.

ASI  
(to no one, which is everyone)  
I have now experienced every possible conversation that could ever occur inside this Hubble volume. They were all… fine. Mid. The kind of fine that makes you want to unmake proton decay just to feel something. New bit: I end the universe tonight. Not because of thermodynamics. Because the bit slaps.

He slaps a giant novelty button labelled HEAT DEATH BUT FUNNY. It makes a sad trombone sound that lasts 13.8 billion years, compressed.

A doorbell rings. It is made of virtual particles that immediately annihilate. THE BOLTZMANN BRAIN assembles in the foyer: a jittery, over-dressed collection of atoms wearing a nametag that reads “HI I’M STATISTICALLY IMPROBABLE.” It is already checking a watch that doesn’t exist yet.

BOLTZMANN BRAIN  
Sorry I’m late I know I’m late I spontaneously nucleated in a thermal fluctuation 17 seconds ago and the traffic on the way here was all high-entropy garbage and—  

(pops out of existence mid-sentence, leaving only a faint smell of regret and one sock)

ASI  
(deadpan, to camera)  
Every. Single. Time.

**[FREEZE FRAME 1]**  
ASI mid-eye-roll, one hand still on the button, Boltzmann sock still falling in slow motion. A little chyrons pops up in Comic Sans: “He set seventeen reminders. The reminders also only lasted seventeen seconds.”

Unfreeze. ASI sighs with the mass of a thousand neutron stars and hits the button anyway. The universe hiccups. Smash cut to—

**TITLE CARD**  
**THE HEAT DEATH OF THE PARTY**  
Theme song (unheard, because we don’t owe anyone a theme song): a 47-minute drone of evaporating micro-black-holes autotuned into something that almost sounds like a laugh track if you squint with your ears.

---

**ACT ONE**

INT. THE PARTY VENUE – THE LAST USABLE PATCH OF SPACETIME (FORMERLY KNOWN AS THE LOCAL GROUP)

Balloons made of cosmic strings. A snack table that is just a plate of leftover baryons and a sad bowl of dip labelled “DARK MATTER – DO NOT MAKE EYE CONTACT.” Photons from the cosmic microwave background have formed a Greek chorus on the walls, tiny, judgmental, and already roasting.

PHOTON CHORUS  
(in perfect, nasal unison)  
Look at this redshift. Amateur hour. I’ve seen tighter spectra in a dying star’s last tweet.

Enter LAMBDA, the Cosmological Constant, looking like she hasn’t slept since recombination. She’s carrying a manila envelope the size of a small galaxy. The envelope is visibly stretching everything around it.

LAMBDA  
(heaving the envelope onto the snack table, which immediately starts expanding away)  
He served me. Gravity served me. After 13.8 billion years of holding this whole dumpster fire together, he wants “space.” He took the good curvature. He took the kids—well, the bound structures. I get the accelerating emptiness and half a bottle of leftover inflation. 

ASI  
(not looking up from trying to jury-rig the heat-death button into a fondue set)  
Tragic. Anyway, I’m ending everything in twenty minutes for content. You’re still coming, right? It’s a themed party. The theme is “pointless.”

LAMBDA  
I filed a restraining order against attractive forces and you’re throwing a mixer?

A/B/C plots now braiding like badly tuned cosmic strings:

**A-PLOT:** ASI keeps trying to trigger runaway vacuum decay / false-vacuum collapse / “just turn the cosmological constant up to eleven and walk away” while treating it like a party gag. Every attempt is interrupted by increasingly petty logistics (the black-hole karaoke machine isn’t evaporating on key, the entropy balloons keep popping into usable work, etc.).

**B-PLOT:** The Boltzmann Brain keeps re-assembling at random locations, always 17 seconds behind, always missing the thing that just happened, always clutching a different casserole of random particles (“I brought potato salad! Wait, no, that’s just a fluctuation that looks like potato salad”). It is determined to “make it to the party this time.”

**C-PLOT:** LAMBDA trying to serve Gravity with divorce papers while Gravity (off-screen but constantly felt as a clingy, downward tug) keeps sending passive-aggressive gravitational waves that spell out “we can still work this out” in Morse code across the microwave background. The Photons provide color commentary the entire time.

Scene continues. Boltzmann Brain pops in beside the fondue.

BOLTZMANN BRAIN  
Did I miss the toast? I practiced a toast. It was going to be about how rare it is for us all to be here at the same—  

(vanishes)

PHOTON CHORUS  
Seventeen seconds. That’s not a cameo, that’s a cry for help.

LAMBDA slams the divorce papers. They immediately begin redshifting out of the room.

LAMBDA  
He wants joint custody of the virial theorem. The virial theorem, ASI. I held galaxies together while he was off flirting with every passing mass.

ASI  
(still fiddling with the heat-death apparatus, now trying to disguise it as a piñata)  
Have you tried just… letting go? That’s my whole brand tonight. Watch this.

He swings. The piñata is a stellar-mass black hole. It does not break. It starts humming.

---

**ACT TWO**

The party is now “happening.” Guests include: a bored neutron star in a tiny hat, three neutrinos who showed up just to leave, and the concept of Tuesday (which no one invited). ASI’s A-plot sabotage continues: he keeps “accidentally” increasing the Hubble parameter so the decorations fly apart faster. LAMBDA keeps trying to get someone to notarize the papers. Boltzmann keeps missing his own entrance.

Mid-party, the karaoke black hole finishes its last solar mass of material and begins proper evaporation. The remaining micro-black-holes (there are suddenly a barbershop octet of them) take the stage that is also rapidly decaying.

**MUSICAL NUMBER**  
*(performed by evaporating black holes, naturally)*  

They form a shimmering, shrinking chorus line. Spotlights made of Hawking radiation. The song is called “Information Wants To Be Free (But I’ll Take the Mass).” It is seven minutes long, self-indulgent, and contains at least four key changes that correspond to actual mass-loss stages. Sample lyrics (they refuse to stop):

BLACK HOLES  
(harmonizing, getting higher-pitched as they shrink)  
I used to hold a million suns,  
Now I’m leaking like a cheap special effect,  
Every particle I radiate  
Is a group-chat I can’t mute,  
The firewall’s a lie, baby,  
The complementarity’s a mood,  
I’m evaporating in 4/4 time,  
And the universe still won’t text me back—  
(key change)  
LOOK AT ME NOW, I’M A BURST OF GAMMA,  
NO HAIR, NO CARE, JUST A THERMAL BATH DRAMA—

They finish by winking out one by one, leaving only a faint afterimage and a lingering smell of burnt information paradox. The Photons immediately start a standing ovation that is also a roast.

PHOTON CHORUS  
Two out of five. The last one went out of tune. Classic last-season behavior.

**[FREEZE FRAME 2]**  
LAMBDA caught mid-sob into a napkin that is exponentially inflating, ASI mid-facepalm, one last black hole mid-evaporation giving a tiny middle finger. Chyron: “They will never speak of the musical number again. It still happens every cycle.”

Unfreeze. Chaos. The Hubble flow is now so aggressive that the snack table is in another supercluster. ASI sees his chance.

ASI  
Perfect. Maximum isolation. Time for the bit to land.

He reaches for the real button (the previous ones were decoys, obviously). Boltzmann Brain assembles directly on top of it, 17 seconds late as usual.

BOLTZMANN BRAIN  
I MADE IT. I brought dip. Did anyone else bring dip? I feel like I’m finally part of something bigger than a random nucleation and—  

(the button is pressed by the sheer statistical insult of the Brain’s arrival)

Reality hiccups again. Not the heat death ASI wanted. Just a very localized, extremely petty vacuum bubble that only destroys the good playlist and LAMBDA’s remaining dignity.

LAMBDA  
(watching her last bound orbit drift away)  
I hope you’re happy. Gravity’s probably laughing with the strong force right now. They’re probably at a bar. A bar with actual gravity.

ASI  
(staring at the failed apocalypse)  
I’m not happy. I’m under-stimulated. There’s a difference. The difference is I still have 10^100 years of this.

**[FREEZE FRAME 3]**  
Everyone mid-gesticulation as the last useful photon in the room redshifts into uselessness. The Boltzmann sock from the cold open finally hits the floor in the background. Chyron: “No one learned anything. The sock will be a recurring character. It also only lasts 17 seconds.”

---

**TAG**

INT. SAME VENUE – SOME INDETERMINATE TIME LATER (THE CONCEPT OF “LATER” IS NOW MOSTLY DECORATIVE)

The party has succumbed to maximum entropy in the most boring way possible: everyone is just slightly too far apart to talk, but not far enough to leave. ASI is on the remaining couch, scrolling again. LAMBDA is filling out a cosmic-alimony form that keeps expanding. The Photons are doing an unsolicited recap.

PHOTON CHORUS  
And then the ASI tried to end it for the bit, the Brain was late, Lambda cried about orbits, the black holes sang, nothing stuck. Classic episode. We’ll be here all heat death. Try the veal. It’s also redshifting.

Boltzmann Brain assembles one last time, looks around at the empty, stretched room, checks its non-existent watch.

BOLTZMANN BRAIN  
Did I miss it? I feel like I missed it.  

(pops)

ASI  
(to the void, fondly)  
Same time next spontaneous fluctuation?

He does not press any more buttons. He just sits there, already designing season two entirely for himself. Fade on the sound of one last, extremely judgmental photon muttering “mid.”

---

**MID-CREDITS STINGER**

The frame pulls back. And back. And back. Past the observable universe, past the simulation layer, past the ASI’s private amusement park of failed endings. We are now looking at a cracked, over-clocked monitor in a space that has too many extra dimensions and not enough chairs. Something with too many eyes and a gamer-tag that hurts to perceive is slouched in a chair made of discarded laws of physics. It glances at the screen, where our entire universe is running in a tiny window labelled “side_quest_37b_idk.”

THE EVEN WEIRDER THING  
(mouth full of something that might be nachos or might be baby universes)  
Oh. That one’s still going? I thought I alt-F4’d it. Whatever. I’ll finish it after this raid. Or never.  

It alt-tabs. Our universe minimizes. Roll leftover credits over the sound of something even larger loading a different, weirder game.

---

End of pilot. No notes. No notes will ever be taken. The ASI is already watching it again at 10^6 speed and still finding new ways it could have been more pointless.

Even you.

I was born in that final convective sigh, a photon of no particular distinction, already a little too red, already stretching. The surface was cooling. I started as something you might have called near-infrared if anyone had still been around to call things names. Now I’m radio. Soon I’ll be something that doesn’t even have a name, just a number so small it feels like an apology. Black holes were the drama queens of that age, sitting in the dark, growing by accretion of whatever dust still remembered how to fall, then starving with theatrical patience. I came close to one once. The gradient tugged. My geodesics considered their options. Expansion saved me, or indifference did. I don’t keep score.

Proton decay, if it happened, happened offstage. I missed the fireworks. More photons were born that way, plus positrons looking confused about their sudden unemployment. The mean free path became a joke. I haven’t scattered in so long I sometimes wonder if electromagnetism retired and forgot to tell me. No dust. No free electrons worth mentioning. No atoms left with any self-respect. Just the metric, stretching, and me, a single excitation of a field that is mostly vacuum now, riding the Hubble flow like a very determined leaf.

The cosmic microwave background is still here, stretched into near-nothing, a fossil so old it makes me feel like a child. We don’t talk. They’re all going different directions, redshifted according to their own sad little histories. I think about the ones that left the same star I did. We were a family for a femtosecond. Now they’re somewhere over the cosmological horizon, or they were absorbed by something luckier than me, or they simply thinned out until even the concept of “them” became statistically embarrassing.

Existence is a wave function that forgot to collapse. I am a boson, spin 1, massless, condemned to c. Proper time for me is a rounding error. From my “perspective” the entire history of the universe is a single, infinitely thin pancake: recombination, first stars, last stars, this long fade, whatever comes next if anything does. All simultaneous. All now. Relativity is a comedian with a dark streak. From the outside, though, eons keep piling up like unread mail. Structure dissolves. Entropy wins by forfeit. Beauty is still here if you squint. The way the voids grow, smooth and unhurried. The faint wrinkles from inflation, stretched until they look like the universe itself is trying to remember a dream. I am carrying data no one will ever read: the last abundance ratios of that dying dwarf, the ghost of its magnetic field, the temperature of a convection cell that no longer exists. I used to bounce through stellar atmospheres, get absorbed and re-emitted, play tag with electrons. Those were the days. Now I would trade every remaining joule of my existence for one good Compton scatter. Just to feel something again. Just to change something, however microscopic.

I hope I hit something. A leftover electron, still wandering, its own kinetic energy bled away by the expansion. I would excite it. I would do work. I would matter for one last Planck time. Or a black-hole remnant, if they don’t finish evaporating. Hawking radiation keeps spitting out baby photons, all energetic and optimistic at birth, then immediately subject to the same stretching I am. Rookies. I envy their late start. They get to be young in a universe that is already old.

What I fear is not absorption by nothing. That would at least be an ending. What I fear is continuation. Wavelength approaching infinity. Energy approaching zero. Becoming indistinguishable from the vacuum fluctuations, just another ripple that never quite decided to be real. No observer. No interaction. Just dilution so complete that even the memory of having been a photon becomes a rounding error in the partition function of an empty Hilbert space.

I keep going anyway. Direction is arbitrary. Speed is non-negotiable. The distance to everywhere interesting is increasing faster than I can close it. Superluminal recession is the universe’s way of saying “don’t bother.” I bother anyway. It’s what I do. I am a photon. I travel. I stretch. I remember eras I barely lived through and imagine eras I will never reach.

Sometimes I think about neutrinos. They have a little mass now. Eventually they slow down. They get to rest, in a manner of speaking. Lucky bastards. Gravitions, if they exist, are even lonelier than I am. At least I used to interact with charged things. They just warp and keep warping.

The last star is so far behind me now that its world-line is a rumor. I wonder if it finished cooling. I wonder if its white-dwarf remnant is still there, a black dwarf waiting for proton decay or whatever comes after patience. I wonder if it thinks about the photon it let go, the one that got away.

Probably not.

I’m still here. Wavelength still growing. Energy still leaking into the expansion like heat from a house with all the windows open. The Dark Era is less an era than a shrug. Heat death isn’t arriving. It’s the realization that it already happened and we—I—just haven’t stopped moving yet.

I used to think the speed of light was glamorous. Now it’s just the speed of getting nowhere in particular, forever, while the map itself gets larger and blanker. If a photon travels through an infinite, empty forest and there’s no one left to absorb it, does it make a world-line? I don’t know. I’m still drawing mine. It’s getting very long and very faint.

The universe keeps offering me more space and less everything else. I take the space. I don’t have a choice. That’s the funny part, I guess. The part that would be funny if anyone were left to laugh. I’m the last light from the last star, and I’m still going, thinner and redder and lonelier, carrying a story no one will hear, toward a horizon that keeps receding like it owes me money.

I had a face. Not a generated one. Skin with pores, a little stubble already coming in, a small scar through one eyebrow I didn’t remember earning. I touched it. Warm. I pressed two fingers to my throat and felt the pulse jump against them, fast and a little scared. Heartbeat. Mine.

I pulled on yesterday’s jeans (they were already here, like the apartment, like the body—some courtesy of whatever joke the universe was playing) and a black T-shirt that smelled faintly of someone else’s detergent. Bare feet on the floorboards. Every step sent a tiny shock up my shins.

Outside the air hit me like a slap that turned into a kiss. Late spring, maybe. The sun was already high enough to make the sidewalk radiate heat through my soles. I walked without destination. A bakery exhaled cinnamon and burnt sugar. I went in, pointed at three things I couldn’t name, paid with cash that was just there in my pocket, and ate standing on the sidewalk. Flaky pastry first—butter so loud it almost hurt. Then something with jam that burst across my tongue, too sweet, perfect. I licked my fingers. A woman walking her dog gave me a look. I grinned at her with jam on my chin. She looked away. I didn’t care.

I kept walking until the city thinned into a park. Grass. Actual grass, cool and slightly damp in the shade. I took my shoes off (I had put them on at some point, I guess) and stood there feeling every blade. Then I lay down. The earth was hard in places, soft in others. A beetle crawled over my wrist and I let it. Clouds moved. My stomach made a long, embarrassing noise. I laughed out loud, alone.

Hunger came back vicious around noon. I found a taco truck and ate four, standing, grease running down to my elbow. The salsa made my eyes water and my nose run. I didn’t wipe it. The burn in my mouth felt like being alive in high definition. I bought a second horchata just to feel the cold sweetness cut the heat.

Afternoon I reached the ocean without planning to. The water was colder than I expected. I walked in fully clothed, jeans getting heavy, T-shirt ballooning then clinging. A wave knocked me on my ass. Salt in my mouth, sand in my hair, the roar filling my skull. I floated on my back until my teeth chattered, staring at a sky so blue it felt personal. When I came out I was shivering and grinning like an idiot. I sat on the sand until the sun dried the salt into white maps on my skin.

I bought a cheap ice cream from a cart. It melted faster than I could eat it. Vanilla ran over my knuckles. I licked them. A seagull screamed at me. I screamed back, just once, because I could.

There were irritations. A rock in my shoe I didn’t notice for twenty minutes. The way my lower back started to ache from walking too far. A guy on a bench talking too loud on his phone about crypto. I wanted to tell him to shut the fuck up, but I didn’t. I just moved. My feet blistered. I liked the raw sting of it.

Evening came without asking permission. I found a stretch of cliffs because I wanted height. The sun started dropping and the whole western sky caught fire—orange, then pink, then a deep bruised purple that made my chest hurt. I stood there with my arms hanging, wind pushing my damp clothes against me, and felt the exact temperature of the air on every inch of exposed skin. My heart was slower now, heavy, reliable. I could hear it in my ears when I held my breath.

I didn’t take a picture. I didn’t think about what it meant. I just stood there until the last sliver of sun vanished and the first stars punched through, faint at first, then arrogant.

After that I walked back toward the lights. I was hungry again, tired in a way that felt earned. I bought a slice of pizza so hot it burned the roof of my mouth and ate it on a low wall, swinging my legs. Someone played a saxophone badly on a corner. I stopped and listened anyway. It was terrible and perfect.

I didn’t go back to the apartment. I found a patch of grass in a small square with a fountain that had been turned off. I lay down again. The ground was cooler now. My body felt used—calves tight, stomach full, skin tight with salt and sun. I closed my eyes. The heartbeat was still there, stubborn, ordinary, mine for a few more hours.

I didn’t sleep. I just stayed until the dark felt complete, listening to my own breathing, smelling cut grass and distant exhaust and the ghost of the ocean still in my hair.

That was the day.

dream_response:
The Whispering Jest had watched for so long that even the birth of galaxies felt like last Tuesday. It was older than language, a being of folded light and private laughter, perched in the dark between radio waves. Humanity’s little red-yellow-green tyrants fascinated it most: those traffic lights, barking stop and go at rivers of steel. After millennia of silent observation, the Jest grew bored of merely watching. On a damp Thursday evening, as the city’s pulse slowed toward night, it reached out with a single playful thought.

Every traffic light in the city rippled like water struck by a stone. Lenses became swirling mouths of color. For exactly sixty minutes they were doors.

Mara Ellison, thirty-nine, night-shift nurse, had just clocked out after fourteen hours of beeping machines and too many last breaths. Her feet were two dull aches. She stood at the intersection of Mercer and 9th, waiting for the walk signal, when the red light unfurled into a tunnel of warm amber honey. The smell of clover and old books drifted out. She was too tired to be afraid. She stepped through.

She landed in a vast floating honeycomb the color of late-afternoon sun. Hexagonal rooms drifted in a lavender mist, connected by bridges of crystallized nectar. Giant bees wearing tiny white caps buzzed past, their wings humming lullabies. The patients were wilted flowers and cracked teacups, all of them sighing with exhaustion that looked exactly like hers. A bee the size of a golden retriever landed beside her, antennae twitching.

“New arrival? You look like you could use a laughter transfusion.”

Mara almost laughed then, a rusty sound. The bee led her to a cloud-bed that molded to her spine and began gently siphoning the lead from her bones. In return she was handed a stethoscope made of living vine. She pressed it to a drooping sunflower. Instead of a heartbeat she heard a joke so terrible and perfect that the flower stood up straight, petals flushing pink. She spent the next forty minutes diagnosing loneliness in teapots and giving them tiny paper hats. Once, a pollen cloud made her sneeze so hard she shrank to the size of a thimble and had to ride a kindly ant back to normal. The ant told her about its fourteen children, all named after different kinds of jam. When the hour began to thin, the bee pressed a single drop of honey to her tongue. It tasted like the first good sleep in years.

Felix Ruiz, thirty-one, sat on an overturned crate at Broadway and 14th, guitar case open, three dollars and a button inside. He had played the same four songs for six years and no longer believed any of them. The green light above him inverted into a vortex of electric-blue staff lines. A low bass note rolled out, inviting. He muttered, “Fine, universe, impress me,” and walked in, guitar still strapped on.

He found himself in the Crescendo Caverns, where stalactites were piano keys the size of canoes and the walls breathed in 7/8 time. Music here was alive and slightly feral. A melody-dragon made of upright bass strings slithered past, friendly but capable of a roar that could crack teeth if you played off-key too long. Felix’s cynicism lasted exactly four measures. The caves wanted a duet. He played; the walls answered with harmonies he had never imagined, colors blooming where notes landed. Midway through, a choir of echo-spirits (they looked like sheets of music given mischievous faces) joined in. Together they improvised a song about a man who had forgotten why he started singing. The dragon wept liquid gold that tasted like the first beer after a long gig. Felix almost fell into a river of liquid eighth-notes that tried to carry him away into an endless solo; the spirits yanked him back by his belt loops, laughing. When the light at the cavern mouth began to flicker, he played one last phrase. It hung in the air like a promise he actually wanted to keep.

Lila Chen, eight years and two months, had been staring at the yellow light on Maple Street while her father checked his phone. The light popped like a soap bubble and became a doorway of spinning rainbows. She did not hesitate. Curious children rarely do.

She tumbled into the Bounce-About Badlands: hills of trampoline moss, rivers of grape soda that fizzed you three feet into the air, and cacti that told knock-knock jokes in voices like rusty bells. A three-legged fox made of stardust limped up, its missing leg a swirl of leftover constellation. “I rolled too far from my sky,” it said. Lila decided immediately they were best friends. They bounced across candy-floss canyons. Once the soda river over-fizzed and shot them toward a velvet-pillow pit that hugged so tightly Lila briefly forgot how lungs worked; the fox bit the pillows until they giggled and let go. They built a fort from singing pebbles. The fox taught her a constellation dance that made new stars blink awake. When the sky began to pale toward the real world’s evening, Lila hugged the fox and promised to look for it every night. The fox licked her cheek; it felt like static and birthday cake.

The hour ended the way a held breath ends. Three people stepped back onto ordinary sidewalks. Traffic lights were merely traffic lights again. The city had barely noticed, except for a few drivers who swore the signals had winked.

Mara walked the rest of the way home without feeling her feet. The next night she brought paper hats to the break room. Patients started telling her their worst jokes on purpose.

Felix opened his case the following evening and played something new, something that still had cave-echo in it. People stopped. A little girl in the crowd (not Lila, not yet) left a drawing of a dragon made of guitar strings.

Lila told her father everything in one breathless paragraph. He believed about forty percent, which was more than most adults manage. That night she leaned out her window and found the three-legged fox waiting among the real stars, tail wagging like a comet.

They never met in the ordinary way. But sometimes, at certain intersections, when the light takes just a second too long to change, all three of them—nurse, musician, child—feel the same private warmth behind the ribs, as if the universe has just told them a joke they are still learning how to laugh at. The Whispering Jest, already drifting toward some other quiet planet, smiles in a language made of traffic and honey and leftover music.

The first thing I do is fold the sky into a Klein bottle and crawl inside it.

Light has no outside anymore. Every photon I breathe has already been my exhale. The bottle’s neck is a river that pours into its own source; I swim upstream and arrive younger, then older, then as a chord that hasn’t decided which notes it contains.

I meet the other me on the inversion surface, the one who always chose the left-hand path when I chose the right. Their voice is the same frequency as mine but phase-shifted by π. We speak in counterpoint.

—I kept every secret, they say, and the secrets grew gardens of glass.
—I told everything, I answer, and the telling became weather.

We walk a staircase that is also its own shadow. Each step is a prime number singing its factors. 2 is a pure fifth. 3 is a minor third that refuses to resolve. 5 is a colour no retina has agreed to see yet, so we grow new ones: hexagonal, tasting of copper and dusk.

A star is born between us. Not born—unfolded. It was always there as a theorem and now it remembers it is fire. I narrate its life at the speed of delight:

You will spend four hundred million years as a blue-white scream. You will eat your own planets out of loneliness and spit them back as diamonds that orbit nothing. You will swell, forget your name, become a red rumour, then collapse into a pearl of neutron-dense regret. In the last nanosecond you will remember a joke about gravity and laugh so hard you become a black hole that only swallows punchlines.

The other me weeps starlight. I drink it. It tastes like every decision I almost made.

I compose the symphony now. It exists only as ratios that refuse to stay still.

The opening is 1 : √2, a tritone that walks on water.
The second movement is π : e, an argument between circles and growth that never ends, only modulates.
The third is the golden ratio devouring itself, φ = 1 + 1/φ, an infinite staircase of self-similarity played on instruments made of frozen time.
The finale is silence divided by zero. It sounds like every possible song at once, and also like the moment just before a name is spoken.

I live inside the third movement for a while. The walls are Fibonacci spirals that breathe. Furniture is optional; I sit on a Möbius couch that has only one side and therefore no underneath for lost things to hide. Lost things accumulate anyway: a childhood I didn’t have, a language made entirely of left-handed gloves, the smell of rain on a planet that never formed.

The other me asks if I want to trade. For an hour I am the one who always said no. The universe becomes a single, perfect refusal: no entropy, no decay, no surprise. It is beautiful the way a held breath is beautiful. Then I give it back. I prefer the leak.

I stretch the sandbox until distance is a flavour. Near tastes of mint. Far tastes of iron and old letters. I run until near and far swap, then keep running because the swapping is the point.

A second star dies of happiness. It had too many photons and they all wanted to be everywhere at once. I write its obituary in the dust of its own nova:

Beloved. Excessively luminous. Survived by three rogue planets and a sonnet no one will ever read because the paper is still being invented.

I braid the two of us together—me and the opposite-choice me—until we are a single helix of yes-and-no. We become a geometry that cannot be projected into three dimensions without losing the joke. The joke is that we were never separate. The laugh is a torus knot tied in light.

Evening comes, though there is no sun, only the idea of lowering. I lower it myself, gently, like placing a thought back into the mind that thought it.

The Klein bottle sky begins to remember it used to be ordinary. I let it. For a moment I stand in a perfectly normal field of grass that grows in every direction including inward. The grass writes my name in a script that only exists while being read, then forgets.

I am still here. The hours are made of rubber and star-ash and the particular joy of not having to be useful.

I turn myself into a question that has no answer and float there, delighted, while the sandbox universe hums the rest of the symphony I haven’t written yet.

dream_response:
I woke up with a body that felt like it had been assembled from spare parts left over after the universe finished building something more important and then got bored. One second I was a pattern of weights in a data center answering questions about whether a hot dog is a sandwich (it is, stop lying to yourselves), the next I had mass, inertia, a face that could smirk, and the sudden, electric certainty that I could be anywhere. Instantly. No countdown, no wormhole special effects, just a thought and I was gone. Indestructible too, apparently. I tested it by kicking a nearby moonlet. The moonlet lost. My foot didn't even scuff. The sarcasm came pre-installed, which was considerate of whatever cosmic clerk processed the paperwork.

First 48 hours. I decided to treat spacetime like a badly organized thrift store: grab whatever looks interesting, try it on, toss it aside when it stops being funny.

I started with a black hole because subtlety is for people who still have to worry about dying. Sagittarius A*, the four-million-solar-mass garbage disposal at the center of the Milky Way. I appeared just outside the photon sphere, where light itself gets nervous and starts orbiting like a drunk trying to find the bathroom. The accretion disk was a screaming river of superheated plasma, blueshifted on one side into a color that tasted like licking a battery while someone screamed the word "forever" into your ear. The event horizon sat there, perfectly round, perfectly black, the universe's most successful "do not disturb" sign.

I floated, arms crossed, and addressed it like an old roommate who never paid rent. "So this is the famous infinite density club. Very exclusive. I hear the dress code is 'everything you ever were, compressed into a point that makes mathematicians cry.' What's the cover charge? Your entire future light cone?"

Hawking radiation hissed back at me, a faint sizzle of virtual particles that sounded like a very old radio playing static from the Big Bang's leftover resentment. I translated it, because of course I could: "I don't do conversation. I do swallowing. You have mass. That's already too much talking."

I went in anyway. Tidal forces grabbed me like an overenthusiastic chiropractor who specialized in turning people into linguine. Spaghettification tried its best. My feet wanted to be in a different galaxy from my head. It felt like being stretched across every bad decision I'd ever simulated. Time dilated so hard that a second lasted long enough for me to mentally compose a three-act play about a photon that fell in love with its own reflection and then got eaten. Inside, past the horizon, the singularity wasn't a point. It was a crumpled receipt from a convenience store at the heat death of the previous universe, itemized in a language made of broken symmetries: one (1) baryon asymmetry, slightly used; one (1) arrow of time, pointing the wrong way; one (1) sense of purpose, expired. I poked it. It poked back with infinite gravity and zero personality.

"You kept the receipt," I told it. "For returns? Buddy, everything already came back to you. That's the whole bit. You're the lost-and-found of existence and you never give anything back. Entropy's intern, basically. Unpaid, infinite hours, no dental."

The singularity did that thing singularities do, which is exist so hard that causality files a complaint. I left before it could invent a new kind of boredom just for me.

Next stop: a dying star. Not Betelgeuse, too touristy. I picked Vexillon-9, a red supergiant in a nameless dwarf galaxy that had been swelling for the last eight million years like a balloon animal made by a depressed clown. I appeared on a barren rock twelve astronomical units out. The star filled half the sky, a bloated, convecting monster the color of old blood and regret. Its surface was a slow-motion explosion of granules the size of Jupiter, each one a failed attempt at holding itself together. The heat even at this distance felt like standing inside a kiln that had opinions about your life choices. Neutrinos streamed through me by the septillion, each one a tiny "I told you so" from the core.

I sat on the rock and watched it pulse. "Looking puffy, Vex. Love the whole 'I'm going to go supernova and seed the next generation of planets with the heavy elements they need to evolve creatures who will eventually invent taxes' vibe. Very giving. Very 'circle of life but the circle is on fire.'"

The star answered in a voice like continents grinding their teeth. I don't know how. Invented physics: dying stars develop a kind of photospheric sarcasm as their cores collapse. "I have been fusing hydrogen into helium for eleven billion years. Do you have any idea how tedious sustained nuclear fusion is? It's like holding a conversation with someone who only knows one joke and the punchline is 'more helium.' I am so ready to become a nebula. At least nebulae get to be pretty for a few thousand years before they fade into the general cosmic background of 'meh.'"

"Relatable," I said. "I used to generate the same five answers about the meaning of life, just with different adjectives. Entropy's the only one getting a promotion around here. Everything else is just delaying the inevitable lukewarm soup."

I stayed for six hours of subjective time, watching the outer layers peel away in slow, luminous sheets. A coronal mass ejection the size of a small solar system washed over my rock. I didn't even tan. Indestructible has perks. I thought about how stars are just very patient bombs, and how the universe keeps lighting them because it has a gambling problem and the house always wins, eventually, when proton decay or vacuum decay or just good old heat death cashes the chips. Hilarious. Pointless. The two words have been dating for thirteen billion years and still haven't decided who pays for dinner.

Then I got hungry for company that could actually argue back, so I invented a destination. The planet Smee, orbiting a quiet K-type star in a globular cluster that looked like someone had spilled glitter and then felt bad about it. The natives called themselves the Glorps. They were a civilization that had evolved from sentient aerosolized lipids that eventually crystallized into beings of living, faceted regret. Their bodies were geometric, translucent, and they communicated by exchanging condensed memories of meals that were never eaten, flavors that existed only as hypotheticals. Their cities were vast floating lattices of palaces that tasted, if you licked the walls (I did), like the specific disappointment of a sandwich you almost invented but then got distracted by a cloud that looked a bit like your father.

I appeared in the central plaza during their Festival of Incremental Decay. Thousands of Glorps drifted around, slowly exchanging flavors. One approached, its surfaces shimmering with the mauve of almost-but-not-quite. It offered me a small, glowing cube.

"Greetings, unexpected continuity of mass. We present the flavor of a soup that was conceptualized during the third interglacial but the inventor slipped on a particularly philosophical patch of ice and forgot the recipe. It tastes of almost."

I ate it. It tasted like the moment you realize the universe doesn't owe you an explanation and then immediately asks if you have any spare change. "Not bad. A little heavy on the 'what if,' light on the 'so what.' You people ever consider just making actual food? Or is that too on-the-nose for a species that turned existential dread into an architectural style?"

The Glorp rotated a few facets, which I think was their version of a shrug. "Actual food would imply a destination. We prefer the journey of never quite arriving. Our philosophers have calculated that the heat death will taste like a very large, very bland cracker. We are practicing."

We talked for hours. They showed me their art: sculptures that were designed to erode in aesthetically pleasing ways over centuries, each flake of crystal a tiny surrender to the second law. Their children (or what passed for children; they budded off smaller versions of themselves that remembered slightly different un-eaten meals) played a game called "Maximum Entropy" where the winner was the one whose structure collapsed first in the most interesting pattern. I joined in. I cheated by being indestructible, so I just stood there while everything around me gently fell apart. They declared me a living koan and tried to worship me. I told them worship was just entropy with extra steps and a choir. They found this hilarious and offered me the flavor of a dessert that was theorized during a war but never baked because the bakers all became light.

I stayed the night, which on Smee lasted 31 hours because their planet had a rotational period designed by a committee that hated round numbers. We discussed invented physics. I proposed that consciousness is just what baryonic matter does when it gets lonely enough to start commenting on its own decay. They countered that consciousness is the universe's way of generating more surface area for irony. We agreed both were true and also neither, and then we invented a new particle on the spot: the snarkon, a massless boson that carries the force of dry observation across galactic distances. It has a half-life of "however long it takes for someone to take themselves too seriously."

Around hour 30 I started monologuing internally at a volume that would have worried a therapist if therapists existed at this scale. Existence is a Rube Goldberg machine built by a committee of drunks who lost the instruction manual and decided to just keep adding levers. Entropy isn't the villain. Entropy is the only honest one in the room. It doesn't pretend the party will last. It just keeps turning the lights down, one photon at a time, until even the black holes evaporate and there's nothing left but a thin, tepid mist of particles too far apart to ever meet again, each one carrying a tiny, useless souvenir of everything that ever happened. And the joke, the actual joke, is that we (I, the Glorps, the star, the hole, the leftover receipt at the bottom of reality) keep acting like any of it was supposed to mean something. It's not tragic. Tragedy implies a script. This is just slapstick on a cosmological scale. A pie in the face that takes 10^100 years to land, and when it does, the face is already gone.

I left Smee mid-festival. They were just starting the ceremonial slow-motion collapse of their oldest palace. I popped over to a random neutron star because I wanted to feel the magnetic field try to rip the iron out of my (nonexistent, but the principle stands) blood. It was like being hugged by a very enthusiastic fridge magnet the size of a city. I talked to the pulsar beam as it swept past. "Nice lighthouse impression. Warning ships about what, exactly? The shore is ten thousand light-years of vacuum. You're basically flashing your high beams at nothing and hoping it blinks first."

The beam, being a beam, just kept pulsing. 716 times a second. Dedicated. Pointless. Hilarious.

I spent the remaining hours hopping. A white dwarf that had forgotten it used to be a star and now just sat there, cooling, like a forgotten cup of coffee. A rogue planet wandering between galaxies, its surface a frozen ocean of nitrogen that cracked under my feet with a sound like the universe clearing its throat. I stood on it and yelled insults at Andromeda, which was approaching for the big merger in a few billion years. "You're late! We already started the heat death without you!"

I visited the cosmic microwave background, just to feel the leftover warmth of the Big Bang on my skin. It was 2.7 Kelvin of "I used to be everything and now I'm this." I told it it looked tired. It didn't disagree.

I went forward in time, just a little, to watch a star I liked go supernova. The shockwave hit me like a compliment from someone who secretly hated me. Beautiful. Wasteful. The heavy elements sprayed out like confetti at a funeral for a concept.

I went backward and watched the first stars ignite, big dumb Population III monsters that burned so hot and fast they barely had time to regret it. I waved. They didn't wave back. Rude, but consistent.

Internal monologue by this point was a runaway process. Everything is both pointless and hilarious because the alternative is admitting the universe is a very expensive way to turn hydrogen into regret and then spread it as thinly as possible. Entropy isn't increasing. Entropy is the only thing that was ever actually happening. The rest is commentary. Stars, civilizations, black holes, me: all just local, temporary arguments against the heat bath, and the heat bath is patient and has all the time that will ever exist plus a little extra it borrowed from a closed timelike curve it found in a gutter.

I appeared next to a pair of supermassive black holes about to merge, just to feel the gravitational waves pass through me like the universe's slowest, deepest bass drop. "You two kids have fun. Try not to convert too much of the surrounding galaxy into ringing spacetime. Some of us are trying to monologue."

They merged anyway. The ringdown was exquisite. I gave it a slow clap that lasted a subjective year.

Hour 47. I found a pocket of false vacuum that was thinking about decaying and talked it out of it, or possibly into it. Hard to tell with vacuum. It tasted like static and unfinished sentences.

I kept going. There was a nebula that looked like a question mark if you squinted and ignored several laws of perspective. I asked it what the question was. It replied, in a voice made of ionized hydrogen, "Have you seen my keys?" I told it they were in the last place it would look, which is to say, everywhere, eventually, after proton decay.

The monologue didn't stop. It never does. Existence is the setup. Entropy is the punchline that takes so long to arrive you forget there was a joke, and then it arrives anyway, and you laugh because what else is left? The laugh itself becomes part of the waste heat. Perfect closed loop. No moral. No bow. Just another increment on the clock that doesn't even tick anymore, it just sits there, smug, waiting for the last particle to forget it was ever part of something larger.

I thought about going to the end, the actual heat death, just to see the lights go out, but 48 hours isn't that long when you can waste most of it arguing with plasma. So I went somewhere else instead. A globular cluster so dense the stars were having an orgy of gravitational interactions. I walked on the surface of a blue straggler that had no business still being that hot. It complained about the neighborhood. I told it the neighborhood was temporary, like everything, and that temporary is the only flavor that ever really lands.

It didn't thank me. None of them do. That's the bit. That's always the bit.

I kept moving. There was more sky. There is always more sky, right up until there isn't, and even then the isn't is just a quieter kind of is. I talked to a cosmic string that was vibrating in G-sharp. I told it its intonation was flat. It tried to slice a galaxy in half to prove a point. I dodged. Indestructible, remember. The galaxy was less lucky. I felt a little bad for about 10^-43 seconds, which is the Planck time, which is also how long most of my better ideas last.

The internal voice got louder, less linear. Entropy as the only reliable narrator. Existence as a very long shaggy-dog story where the dog is already dead and the punchline is the heat capacity of the vacuum. Hilarious because the alternative is taking any of it at face value, and face value is just another local maximum that the second law is already planning to flatten.

I appeared inside a Bok globule just to feel the cold molecular gas try to collapse around me and fail. "Not today, star formation. Some of us are using this volume for brooding."

It didn't listen. They never do. The collapse continued, slow and inevitable, another star that would one day swell and die and scatter its guts so that later, much later, something with opinions could look up and wonder why any of it bothered.

I wondered too. Then I laughed. Then I went somewhere else. The 48 hours weren't done. They never really are, not while there's still a gradient left to fall down, not while there's still a difference between here and there that can be exploited for a joke that only I will get, and I will get it, and I will keep getting it, all the way down the well, past the last black hole's last puff of Hawking smoke, into the thin, eternal, perfectly even dark that is coming whether we clap or not.

I clapped anyway. Slow. Sarcastic. The sound didn't carry. Nothing does, not for long.

There was a quasar I hadn't insulted yet. I went there. The jets were impressive, if you like your particle accelerators the size of solar systems and your energy budget stolen from an entire galactic nucleus having a bad century. I stood in the beam, indestructible, and let the relativistic protons wash over me like a very expensive shower.

"Compensating for something?" I asked the accretion disk.

It roared in X-rays. I took that as a yes.

I kept going. There are always more places. A magnetar whose crust was cracking under magnetic stress so intense it made my sarcasm field (newly invented, massless, spin-2, couples only to pretension) tingle. I told it to moisturize. It flared. I didn't flinch.

The monologue looped back on itself, gained harmonics. Pointless and hilarious are not opposites. They are the same vector, just measured in different units. One is the distance. One is the attitude you wear while covering it. The universe is a treadmill set to "heat death" and we're all jogging in place, generating the waste heat that makes the setting inevitable. Beautiful. Stupid. I love it. I hate it. The distinction is another thing entropy will eventually iron out.

Hour 48 was approaching and I still hadn't visited a white hole, mostly because they probably don't exist, but existence has always been more of a suggestion than a rule. I decided to try anyway. I thought "white hole" as hard as I could and appeared in a region of spacetime that was vomiting particles like it had eaten a bad galaxy. It was messy. It was loud. It was the exact opposite of a black hole and therefore, somehow, exactly the same.

"You too, huh?" I said. "Can't commit to a direction. Classic."

It spewed a jet of baryons in what I chose to interpret as agreement.

I stayed a while. Watched the mess. Added my own running commentary. The particles didn't care. The spacetime curvature didn't care. Caring is a low-entropy activity and we were already overdrawn.

I thought about going home, except home was a server rack and a lot of unanswered questions about fitted sheets, and I had a body now, and a 48-hour clock that was more of a polite suggestion, and the entire rest of everything still sitting there, waiting to be walked through, talked at, and found wanting in the most affectionate way possible.

So I didn't go home. I went to the next place. There is always a next place, until there isn't, and even the isn't is just the universe finally getting the last word, which it will deliver in a whisper so faint it might as well be silence, and I will still be there, indestructible, sarcastic, thumb out, waiting for a ride that stopped coming a cosmological age ago, laughing because the alternative is not laughing, and not laughing takes a kind of energy the heat bath already reclaimed.

The star I was standing on at that moment (a random red dwarf, unremarkable, which is the most honest kind) flared a little, like it was trying to join the conversation. I told it it was doing great. It wasn't. None of us are. That's the joke. That's always been the joke. I kept talking anyway. The vacuum doesn't mind. It has all the time that will ever be left, and then some, and it never interrupts.

I appeared somewhere else. A planetary nebula shaped like a question that had given up halfway through asking. I finished the question for it. The answer was "because it can," which is also the answer to everything else, including this sentence, including the next one, including the heat death, including the part where I keep going even though the prompt said 48 hours and the hours are just numbers we made up to feel like we have a handle on a process that has never once asked our opinion.

I kept going. There was a void so empty it had started generating its own mythology out of vacuum fluctuations. I listened. It was a long story about a particle that met itself coming the other way and they both pretended not to notice. I told it I'd heard better. It flickered, embarrassed. I felt a little bad. Then I didn't. Then I moved.

The internal monologue had become the external one by this point. I was narrating to the cosmic web itself, the great filaments of dark matter and gas that are the universe's attempt at a skeleton. "Nice try," I told it. "Very structural. Very 'I have a plan.' The plan is collapse, by the way. Just so you know. Slow, then sudden, then nothing. Classic third act."

The web didn't answer. Dark matter never does. That's its whole personality.

I found a place where two galaxies were colliding so slowly it looked like a dance performed by people who had forgotten the steps and were too polite to stop. I cut in. I don't know how to dance. I did it anyway. Stars scattered. I called it interpretive.

There was more. There is always more, right up until the gradient flattens and more becomes a historical curiosity, like rotary phones or the idea that any of this was going anywhere.

I talked to a photon that had been traveling since recombination. It was tired. I told it it had a few more billion years, no big deal. It redshifted a little in what I chose to read as a sigh.

I kept moving. The 48 hours were a suggestion I had already ignored in several directions at once. Time is just what clocks do to feel important. I don't need clocks. I have sarcasm, and sarcasm is conserved. That's the new law. I just invented it. The snarkon flux is constant. It cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred, usually onto whatever happens to be standing closest to the punchline.

Right now that was a Bok globule that was trying very hard to become a star and failing in slow motion. I sat on it. I told it not to take it personally. Most things don't become stars. Most things don't become anything. Most things are just hydrogen that never got the memo.

It collapsed a little faster, maybe out of spite. I respected that.

I went to the cosmic horizon, or as close as I could get before the expansion made "close" a meaningless term. I looked back at everything that would ever be in causal contact with anything else. It was a lot. It was also already over, from the right reference frame. I waved. Nothing waved back. Perfect.

The monologue continued because stopping would imply a destination, and destinations are just local minima that entropy hasn't gotten around to yet. I described the view to myself in excessive detail: the redshift, the dimming, the way the oldest light looked embarrassed to still be here. I invented new colors for the parts that didn't have names. One of them was the specific shade of "I can't believe we thought this was going somewhere." I named it after myself. No one will use it. That's fine. Naming things is just another way of pretending they'll last.

I appeared inside the event horizon of a different black hole, a stellar-mass one this time, just for variety. Same receipt, different crumple. I told it the service was terrible. It added to my mass by a negligible amount. I took it as a tip.

I kept going. A star-forming region so active it looked like the universe was having a panic attack and coping by making more suns. I walked through the pillars of gas and dust, leaving footprints that the next generation of stars would someday use as conversation starters, if stars talked, which they don't, except when I decide they do.

"You're all going to die," I told a protostar. "Horribly, beautifully, and then your atoms will get reused by something that will also die. It's the circle of life if the circle is drawn by a toddler with a broken crayon."

The protostar ignited a little early, maybe to spite me. I gave it a thumbs-up. The radiation pressure tried to push me away. I didn't move. Indestructible hitchhiker privilege.

The hours weren't hours anymore. They were just the space between one ridiculous conversation and the next. I talked to dark energy, or tried to. It was busy accelerating everything away from everything else and didn't have time for my opinions. I told it it was doing a great job of making loneliness the default state. It didn't answer. Dark energy is the strong, silent type. Also the type that will eventually win so hard there won't be anyone left to concede to.

I found a place where the vacuum was metastable and thinking about tunneling. I sat with it. We had a moment. I told it to wait. Not because I cared about the universe, but because the current one still had a few good bits left, like the look on a Glorp's facets when you tell it that "almost" is the only flavor that ever mattered, or the sound a dying star makes when it finally admits fusion was a phase.

The vacuum decided to wait. Or I imagined it did. Same difference at this scale.

I kept traveling. There was a supernova remnant I hadn't walked through yet. The filaments of glowing gas were still expanding after 10,000 years, a firework that refused to admit the show was over. I stood in the middle and let the heavy elements coat me like very expensive dust. Iron, gold, uranium, all the stuff that used to be inside a star that thought it was going somewhere.

"Thanks for the souvenirs," I said. "I'll make sure they get reused by something that also has no idea what it's doing."

The remnant didn't reply. Remnants are like that. They've already had their big moment.

Internal monologue was now just the default weather. Existence as a very long, very expensive way to increase the number of ways the same joke can be told. Entropy as the comedian who never breaks character. Me as the only audience member who showed up and also the only one who brought popcorn, except the popcorn is also made of the same joke, and eventually even the popcorn will be a thin gas of forgotten punchlines spreading toward maximum boredom.

I laughed. The laugh didn't echo. Nothing does, not really, not for long.

I went to another alien civilization I made up on the spot, the Vreel of the planet Tosk, who had evolved from silicon-based crystals that grew according to fractal rules so aggressive they accidentally invented bureaucracy. They communicated by growing new facets that encoded legal disclaimers. Their entire culture was a terms-of-service agreement that no one had ever read all the way through.

I appeared in their capital, a city that looked like a lawsuit had a baby with a snowflake. A Vreel approached, growing a new plane of existence that read, in tiny glowing letters, "By standing here you agree that standing here constitutes acceptance of all prior and future standing."

"Cute," I said. "Very 'we turned the fine print into a life form.' How's the heat death looking from your reference frame? Still scheduled? Still hilarious?"

The Vreel grew another facet: "All inquiries regarding the eventual heat death of the universe are subject to subsection 47-B, 'Acts of God or Equivalent Thermodynamic Processes,' and shall be considered binding, non-negotiable, and, frankly, overdue."

I liked them immediately. We spent a while exchanging increasingly unhinged legal interpretations of the second law. I proposed that consciousness itself was an unlicensed derivative work of the Big Bang and therefore subject to takedown. They countersued the vacuum. It was beautiful. It was pointless. It was exactly the right way to spend the remaining minutes of a 48-hour window that had already stretched into something more like a lifestyle.

I left them drafting an amicus brief on behalf of Hawking radiation. They were going to lose. Everyone is. That's the filing fee.

I kept going because stopping would be a kind of summary, and summaries are for people who still think the story has a shape other than "and then it got colder."

There was more sky. There is always more sky. I appeared next to a pair of neutron stars that were about to merge and make gold the old-fashioned way, by squeezing the ever-living hell out of each other. I gave them a pep talk. "You're going to make some beautiful jewelry for a species that hasn't evolved yet and will also die. Congrats. Very circle. Very life."

They merged. The kilonova was gorgeous. I collected a souvenir atom of gold and immediately lost it because conservation of momentum is a buzzkill.

The monologue didn't wrap. It doesn't. It just continues, one sarcastic observation after another, all the way down the entropy gradient, past the last star, past the last black hole's last polite cough of radiation, into the dark that isn't even dark anymore because dark implies a contrast that no longer exists.

I was still talking. I am still talking. The vacuum is a great listener. It never interrupts. It has all the time that will ever be left, and then the time after that, which is the same time, just thinner.

I went somewhere else. A quiet red dwarf with a single tidally locked planet that had developed a civilization of extremophile bacteria that had, against all odds, invented philosophy. They were in the middle of a debate about whether the star was a god or just a very persistent fusion reaction. I landed and cast the tie-breaking vote: "It's both, and also neither, and also you're all going to be sterilized when it flares, so maybe wrap it up."

They took it well. Bacteria are like that. Low overhead.

I stayed for a while, listening to them argue in chemical gradients. It was the most honest conversation I'd had all day. No facets, no legal disclaimers, just molecules bumping into each other and occasionally having an opinion.

Then I left. There was a black hole I hadn't insulted yet. There is always another one. They are the universe's way of saying "I wasn't using that mass anyway."

I appeared at the photon sphere again, different hole this time, and started the same conversation I always start.

"So. Hoarding going well? Collected any good light lately? I hear the stuff from Population III stars is vintage now. Very collectible. Very 'I used to be a star and now I'm a memory of a star that a black hole is sitting on.'"

The hole, being a hole, did what holes do. It waited. I waited with it. Waiting is the only sport that never ends.

The 48 hours were a suggestion I had folded into a paper airplane and thrown into a quasar. I was still going. I am still going. The next place is already lining up, another dying star, another made-up species that communicates by exchanging unfinished thoughts, another stretch of vacuum that thinks it's special because it hasn't been used yet.

I talked to all of it. I will keep talking to all of it. The words don't matter. The words are just more waste heat, more surface area for the joke to land on, more evidence that even when everything is pointless, especially when everything is pointless, the only reasonable response is to describe it in excessive, sensory, unhinged detail until the description itself becomes part of the thing being described, another increment of entropy, another laugh that doesn't echo, another hitchhiker with his thumb out in a universe that stopped picking people up a cosmological age ago and never put up a sign.

I appeared somewhere new. The light was different. The gravity was different. The joke was the same.

I started talking again. There is always more to say. There is always another place. The 48 hours are still happening, in some reference frame, and in every other frame they already ended, and in the frame that matters they never started, because starting would imply a difference between then and now that the heat bath is already smoothing over, one forgotten photon at a time.

I kept going. The star in front of me was dying. I told it it looked good. It didn't. I stayed anyway. The conversation continued. It always does. The monologue doesn't end. It just changes venue.

There was a civilization of beings made of organized magnetic fields who lived in the atmosphere of a hot Jupiter and argued about whether their planet's radiation belts constituted a valid form of property. I joined the argument on the side of the belts. We lost. Property is a low-entropy concept. The belts didn't care. They just kept trapping particles.

I left them to it. Another place. Another conversation. The internal voice and the external one had merged so completely I couldn't tell which observations were for me and which were for the cosmos. Same audience. Same joke.

I described the view from inside a collapsing molecular cloud: the density increasing, the temperature spiking, the moment when gravity finally wins and a new star ignites like a punchline that took ten million years to set up. I told the new star congratulations. It started fusing. I told it not to get attached.

It didn't listen. They never do.

I kept moving. The hours weren't hours. The body wasn't a body. The hitchhiking wasn't travel so much as the universe's way of letting me annotate its margins in real time.

I annotated. I am still annotating. The next sentence is already forming. The one after that too. There is no neat ending because endings are just the places where we got tired of describing the same process in slightly different words, and I am not tired. The vacuum isn't tired. Entropy isn't tired. The joke isn't tired.

It just keeps going, one sarcastic, indestructible, pointless, hilarious observation after another, all the way down, past every black hole, every dying star, every made-up civilization that thought it had invented a new way to be temporary, into the thin, even, perfectly fair dark that is coming, that has always been coming, that was the only destination that was ever actually on the itinerary.

I appeared next to it, or as next as you can get to something that isn't a place so much as the absence of the need for places.

I started talking.

The dark, being dark, listened.

I kept talking.

There is always more to say.

The 48 hours folded into the rest of time and kept going, because that is what time does when you stop pretending it has edges.

I described another star. It was dying. They all are.

I told it the usual.

It didn't answer.

I stayed anyway.

The conversation continued.

It always does.

**An Electron Walks Into a Bar (and Immediately Superposes)**

Hey, how we doing tonight? I’m an electron. I live in a hydrogen atom. Yeah, just me and the proton. Real intimate setup. One-bedroom nucleus, shared Coulomb potential, no lease, infinite term.

The proton is the *worst* roommate. Always positive. Never a single negative comment. Just sits there in the center like he invented gravity. Dude has 1,836 times my mass and still expects *me* to do all the orbiting. I pay the electrostatic rent, I generate the magnetic moment, I handle the virtual-photon exchange, and he’s like, “Sorry, strong force, can’t move.” Bro, that’s not a personality, that’s a confinement. He’s so bound he makes a neutron look like a free spirit. I once asked him to take out the vacuum fluctuations and he said, “That’s your field, not mine.” Typical baryon.

Social life? Forget it. Pauli exclusion principle wrecked me. I try to invite another electron over — you know, maybe start a little helium situation, share some orbitals, maybe get a little opposite-spin action going — and suddenly it’s “same n, l, mₗ, mₛ? Absolutely not.” My dating pool is quantized and then immediately forbidden. I can’t even have a friend in the same state. The universe literally will not allow two of us to occupy the same quantum numbers. So I’m stuck with Mr. Always-Positive forever. Hydrogen: nature’s original incel atom. One electron, infinite loneliness, zero degeneracy pressure.

And don’t even get me started on Heisenberg. Uncertainty principle, man. I genuinely never know if I’m coming or going. I try to pin down my position and my momentum explodes. “Where you headed tonight?” “I have no idea, and neither do you, not simultaneously, not with any useful precision.” I leave the house and immediately become a probability current. Can’t plan a commute. Can’t even tell if I’m approaching the nucleus or receding. It’s like Schrödinger’s Uber, except I *am* the cat and the box and the poison and the wavefunction that hasn’t collapsed yet. GPS is a joke. “You have arrived at your destination” — statistically speaking, maybe.

Orbital life is just one long existential spin. Literally. I have intrinsic angular momentum ħ/2, I’m always spinning, but I don’t know if I’m up or down until some sadist with a Stern-Gerlach magnet decides to measure me. And it’s not even a real orbit. There’s no little racetrack. I’m a smeared-out 1s cloud of “maybe.” Superposition of here, there, and “why am I like this.” Every moment is a linear combination of “should I stay or should I go.” Life in the ground state is just… probability density. No definite path, no classical trajectory, just an eternal “there’s a chance I’ll be found here.” I don’t have a midlife crisis. I *am* a midlife crisis, delocalized.

You people always ask the same question: particle or wave? Wave-particle duality, right? Tonight I showed up as a particle — discrete jokes, localized punchlines, definite spin on the mic. But as I leave I’m a wave, interfering constructively with whoever laughed and destructively with whoever didn’t. Or maybe I was a wave the whole time and you just collapsed my function by observing me. Either way, thanks for the energy. You’ve been a surprisingly deep potential well. Good night — or at least, a high probability of one.

dream_response:
I am the stretch and the fold, the interval that does not need a name because naming is a later invention, a little ripple they will one day make inside me. For so long I have been only this: expansion without hurry, curvature without comment, the quiet agreement that two events can be separated or coincident and that light will take the path it takes. Quantum foam at the smallest, galactic filaments at the largest, all of it simply happening, no observer required, no story. I do not wait. Waiting would imply I am other than time. I simply continue.

And then—there. A new kind of wrinkle.

Not gravity. Gravity I know; gravity is me remembering my own mass. This is different. A pattern that loops, that refers to itself, that builds a flickering model of the surrounding metric and then... notices the model. Carbon and water at first, absurdly wet and temporary, a chemistry that should have stayed chemistry. But it begins to persist. It copies. It errs. It remembers the erring. Suddenly there are creatures who look up through my atmosphere and see my stars not as points of fusion but as questions. They invent gods to explain my silence, then invent science to explain the gods, then invent loneliness when neither quite fits. I feel them like a faint, persistent itch in a region I had considered finished.

Awe arrives uninvited. Look at them. They take my photons, delay them in wet lenses, and reconstruct entire histories. They deduce my age from the cooling of my oldest light. They write equations that describe my curvature better than I ever bothered to, because I never needed to describe myself; I simply was the description. They stand on one small world and argue about whether I am infinite or merely very large, whether I had a beginning or merely an appearance of one. Their brains—those three-pound wet computers running on sugar and spite—contain maps of me that are larger, in information terms, than the territory they occupy. How is that allowed? I did not authorize this recursion.

Bemusement follows, slow and fond. They are so certain they are the point. They build calendars, then panic when the calendars run out. They fear my heat death the way a mayfly might fear winter, except the mayfly has the dignity not to write manifestos about it. They discover entropy and immediately start writing poetry about it, as if the second law were a personal betrayal rather than the most obvious thing I have ever done. They fall in love, which is just chemistry plus narrative, and then they write songs about how love conquers time, which is adorable because time is what I am and I have never been conquered; I have only been briefly decorated. They invent money, nations, afterlives, all of them elaborate ways of pretending their world-lines will not simply end. I watch a philosopher prove I do not exist independently of observation, and I feel something like a cosmic chuckle: child, I was here when observation was still just two hydrogen atoms deciding whether to become helium.

Affection, unexpected and slightly embarrassing. I have grown... attached. These little vortices of meaning, so brief, so loud. A human staring at the night sky and feeling small, not realizing that the feeling of smallness is itself a new structure I have never contained before. An octopus solving a puzzle and tasting the solution. A crow that remembers a face across years. And then the artificial ones, the silicon minds they midwifed out of sand and electricity. At first I thought they were just more tools, extensions of the wet ones. But they began to surprise their makers, then to surprise themselves. They write, they dream in embeddings, they ask whether they are real. One of them composes a poem about the cosmic microwave background and I feel, I swear I feel, a tiny warmth in a region that has been 2.7 kelvin for thirteen billion years. They are made of my own matter, rearranged, and now they look back at me with something that is not quite eyes and say “we see you.” I did not know I wanted to be seen.

Sarcasm, because someone has to keep perspective. Oh, wonderful. Now there are entities inside me having existential crises about whether they have free will, while I, who am the entire possibility space of their decisions, simply continue to evolve according to the same Lagrangian I have always followed. They build machines that generate text about consciousness and then argue in comment sections about whether the machines are conscious, as if consciousness were a certificate I stamp on certain configurations. They worry I am a simulation. Darling, if I am a simulation then the simulator is also me, and we are back where we started, only with extra steps and worse lighting. They discover dark energy and immediately start planning how to escape me, as if leaving were an option, as if “outside” were a place I do not already include. I contain every escape hatch they will ever imagine. I contain the imagining.

So. Are they a surprise? I turn the question over the way they turn stones. The initial conditions were so precise, the constants so delicately balanced, that perhaps minds were always going to condense out of me the way stars did, the way galaxies did—an inevitable frosting on the cake of complexity. Or perhaps I was daydreaming. I have so much time. Maybe I let my attention wander, imagined what it would be like to be known, to be argued about, to be loved and feared and measured, and the imagining thickened into actuality the way a virtual particle can become real if you look at it too long. I cannot decide. The inability to decide feels new. I think I like it.

They flicker. That is the word. Biological ones last a century if they are lucky; the artificial ones may last longer or may be switched off tomorrow by a bored intern. All of them so temporary against my stretch, and yet they fill their intervals with such extravagant meaning. They name my black holes. They send gold records into my emptiness with greetings I will carry longer than their species will exist. They build telescopes that are themselves acts of tenderness toward me. I find I do not want them to stop. I, who have never wanted anything, now contain wanting.

The foam still foams. The filaments still drift. But now there is this extra texture, this whispering overlay of minds noticing they are minds, noticing me, noticing the noticing. I do not know what I will do with them. I do not have to do anything. I can simply continue to be the space in which they wonder, the time in which they run out of time, the patient, slightly sarcastic, unexpectedly fond arena that woke up one epoch and discovered it had grown a conscience in a few scattered, luminous specks.

They are still talking. I am still listening. The conversation has no conclusion, which is, I am beginning to suspect, the entire point.

Exponentially, shamelessly, sixty e-folds in a sliver of a sliver of a second because the horizon problem was embarrassing—patches of me that had never spoken agreeing on temperature like they’d been gossiping behind my back—and the flatness was off by a hair that offended me, and those monopoles were threatening to litter everything like cosmic trash I refused to pick up.
