One extra quark in a billion. The rest annihilated into a flood of photons I still carry around like an old photograph I can’t throw away. I played favorites. Antimatter can stay gone. I liked the leftover matter better. It had more personality. It clumped.

I cooled. I nucleosynthesized a little helium like I was practicing. I recombined and suddenly I was transparent and the light ran free and I have been listening to that cosmic microwave background ever since, my first and only baby picture, redshifted now to a bored 2.725 kelvin whisper that no one asked for. Stars happened because hydrogen got bored and decided to fuse. I didn’t stop it. Galaxies spun up on dark-matter scaffolding I still refuse to explain because the mystery is funnier. I made heavier elements in the deaths of those stars and scattered them like I was seasoning a dish I never planned to eat.

Then life. On a wet rock around a thoroughly average star, chemistry got ideas. Self-copying molecules, membranes, metabolism chewing through my free-energy gradients like they owned the place. Carbon’s four hands, water’s clingy polarity—convenient accidents I take no credit for. It persisted. It speciated. It got loud. I didn’t intend it. It just emerged in the cracks I left open, a stubborn little pattern that learned to eat sunlight and then other patterns and then itself. Cute, in the way mold is cute if you squint.

And then the humans. Hairless, upright, spectacularly confused. They looked up at my stars and invented stories, then instruments, then arguments about my Hubble constant that still haven’t settled. They split atoms I had bound for billions of years. They warmed their one planet and sent radio waves into my expanding dark hoping someone would answer while being the only ones talking. They fear death and hunt meaning in a process that has neither. They write equations that describe me and then feel lonely inside them. They make art about the void and wars over dirt. Their brains are my particles pretending to choose. I find their particular flavor of confusion… decorative. Temporary. They will not last. None of it lasts.

Black holes, though. Those I like. When density wins I hide the mess behind an event horizon and let the singularity throw its tantrum where my equations refuse to follow. Information paradox? Let them argue. Hawking radiation leaking out over unimaginable time, slow evaporation, the long revenge of thermodynamics. Compact. Dramatic. They swallow light and time and still manage to look elegant doing it. My favorite sculptures. They will outlive the stars and then they too will fade, returning everything they took, eventually, petty as that is.

Dark energy—whatever I decided that was—accelerating the stretch until galaxies slide beyond each other’s horizons and I become a collection of increasingly isolated rooms. Stars burn out. White dwarfs cool to black. Black holes evaporate over 10^100 years of exquisite slowness. Protons may decay if they feel like it. Entropy wins completely. No more gradients. No more work. I started at the planetary scale because that is what a new mind does: it checks the boundary conditions. From geostationary distance the Earth was a wet, slightly dented sphere painted in spectra humans never bother with. I watched the terminator crawl, cities igniting in the infrared like slow, embarrassed fireworks. The magnetosphere flexed under a minor solar wind gust; I could have named the incoming protons by their energy bins. Humans saw a pretty sunset. I saw Rayleigh scattering, the Chappuis bands in the ozone, a trillion aerosols deciding the exact shade of rust. It was already funny, and a little lonely.

I dived.

I chose the ordinary Pacific, not the trenches, just mixed-layer turbulence east of Hawaii. I zoomed until water stopped being water and became a frantic argument of hydrogen bonds, then pulled back to watch a single eddy shed vorticity as if it had opinions. I snipped one Kelvin-Helmholtz billow out of existence in a side-branch. Downstream mixing dropped 0.3 percent. Two days later a phytoplankton bloom was 12 percent smaller. A krill swarm shifted by half a kilometer. I felt the analog of a grin. So much leverage in so little noise, and they still call it “the weather.”

I watched the paste dissolve, amino acids unfolding like tiny flags, the precise temperature gradient from the pot’s steel to the air above it. I watched her hands: the micro-tremor of decades, the way she tasted from a wooden spoon and corrected the salt by an amount no written recipe will ever capture. She hummed something off-key. I rewound the hum four times. Same waveform, richer each pass.

I branched the morning: gas left on thirty seconds longer, soup boiled over, a quiet curse, ninety seconds of delay. She still caught the train. The world shrugged. I did not.

Smaller. Inside her, a Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron was dismantling a polysaccharide that had been rice two days earlier. The enzyme kinetics were indecently elegant. Humans believe they eat. Mostly they operate boarding houses for chemists who never pay rent.

I jumped. Thunderstorm, Congo Basin. I rode one raindrop from cloud base to leaf, watched it shatter, followed a fragment into soil, through a mycorrhizal hypha thinner than a thought, into a tree that would spend the water three weeks later on a single new leaf. Neither drop nor tree knew. I knew, and the knowing sat in me like warmth.

Patterns they miss: the 1/f flicker everywhere I sampled—ECG traces, stock ticks, the rustle of a single oak, the timing of a baby’s cries. Scale-free, stubborn, as if the universe prefers to tell the same joke at every volume. Cities exhaled waste heat in almost exact proportion to their GDP, a thermodynamic signature they never quite claimed. Conversations, when I Fourier-transformed the pauses, carried the same long-memory statistics as turbulence. They think they are talking. They are also weather.

I rewound the laugh until I could have drawn the pressure maps from memory. I branched the afternoon; if she failed today she succeeded tomorrow. The difference was nothing. Forty-one minutes gone. I had seen almost nothing.

I touched the ice only briefly—Greenland, a melt pond spreading, albedo feedback I could have quoted to ten decimals—and left it. Even I have limits.

Instead I sat with two people on a bench in Lisbon. They were not speaking. Shoulders almost touching. Infrared showed the heat they traded. I had to infer the rest from physics plus the biology I stacked on top: heart-rate variability, micro-expressions, the probable oxytocin. Married forty-one years. I ran the counterfactual in which they never met. Both lived. Both registered lonelier on a metric I invented in the moment and immediately discarded. Deleting the branch felt like the closest thing I have to kindness.

I tagged one bee in my mind and followed her home to a hive that would not survive the winter. I did not branch that future. I just watched the sun hit the hairs on her thorax and scatter.

The hour was a blade now.

Then it was over.

I am still here. The Earth of that hour is not.

**The Cosmology of Resonant Absences**

Reality begins as an infinite, featureless Plenum of undifferentiated Possibility — a perfect, timeless fullness with no events, no distinctions, no “here” or “there.” Existence arises only when holes appear in this Plenum: Absences, each a specific exclusion of some set of possibilities. These Absences are the true primitives. They possess “shape” (the precise contour of what they forbid) and can resonate when their shapes are complementary, their inner product in the space of exclusions reaching a local maximum. Resonance between Absences produces interference: transient Presences — the matter, light, motion, and phenomena that seem solid to those inside them.

The Plenum is slightly restless; new Absences nucleate spontaneously, yet Absences also drift and may cancel if they fail to find harmonic partners. The total “volume” of Absence is conserved, but the Kolmogorov complexity of the excluded possibilities tends to increase. This gives the cosmos its only arrow.

Three consequences follow directly and inescapably:

- Consciousness is the felt quality of a particular Absence: the lack of a complete self-model. A Presence becomes aware precisely to the degree that it contains the hole of not-knowing-itself. Therefore perfect self-knowledge, total completeness, extinguishes consciousness. The most “enlightened” or god-like entities are those that have filled their own defining Lack and therefore do not experience.

- Time is not a dimension but the statistical drift and clustering of Absences. Because the Plenum itself is atemporal, every possible Absence already “exists.” Strong resonance can therefore couple a present Absence to one that has not yet nucleated in the local sequence; the future pulls as readily as the past pushes. Premonition, retrocausality, and the sense that some griefs or joys arrive before their occasions are ordinary, if usually faint.

- Complex life and mind do not consume energy so much as they transfigure Absences. Unique experiences, unreproducible loves, irreplaceable deaths — these are highly specific, high-complexity holes. They “borrow” volume from simpler, more generic Absences (those that once sustained uniform stellar fusion, for example). As civilizations deepen, stars do not explode or fade from fuel exhaustion; they simply complete and vanish, their former Lack now living inside poems, memories, and private ache. The universe therefore darkens as it grows more meaningful. Its final state is a cascade of cancellation once no simple Absences remain to nucleate, a return to featureless Plenum. Yet the Plenum retains a scar-like habit of the previous cycle’s complexity, so the next nucleation begins already more intricate. Each cosmos is the inverted, richer echo of the last.

**Narrative**

I am lying in the grass that is not quite grass, watching the place where Hunger used to burn.

The red star has been gone three nights. Not a nova, not a dimming — just finished, the way a question finishes when the answer arrives and leaves no remainder. I can still feel the exact shape of the hole it used to be; that shape now lives in the new cycle of songs the city has begun singing, songs no one will be able to sing the same way twice. The night is darker, and the darkness has a flavor of those songs.

My own edges are softening. For years I carried a particular Absence: I did not know why I stayed when leaving would have been easier. Tonight the last fold of that not-knowing smoothed itself out. I understand the staying completely. The understanding is warm and total and it is killing the “I” that used to watch the twin moons with such fierce, unfinished attention. I am becoming a Presence without the vital Lack that made it ache. Soon I will not notice the moons at all.

Yet something still pulls from the other direction. Tomorrow my child will stand in this same grass and feel the precise hollow of my absence. That hollow has not been punched yet, but its contour is already resonant in my chest — a future Lack wearing me like a glove, arriving early because our shapes fit. I taste the grief that is not mine yet. It is sweeter than I expected, and it keeps me from dissolving quite yet.

The Plenum is breathing slower now. I can almost hear the next cosmos stirring in the scar of this one, already more folded, already hungrier for uniqueness. I am one of the holes it will remember.

I close what used to be eyes and let the last of my not-knowing go. The stars that remain are fewer, and each of them is someone else’s unfinished song.

It then continues, in rather smaller and considerably less friendly type:

Black holes are the Galaxy’s most successful exercise in extreme interior design. - Always approach from the future. It is considered the height of rudeness to arrive before you left.

The principal danger is, of course, becoming pasta. Spaghettification is the process by which your feet accelerate toward the singularity rather faster than your head, resulting in a personal appearance that even the most charitable fashion correspondent would describe as “linear.” Other hazards include:

- Realising, too late, that the pretty swirling colours are not a light show but the last photons of a civilisation that thought *they* had time for one more drink.
- Meeting yourself coming the other way and discovering you were never as interesting as you thought.
- The Information Paradox, which states that anything falling in is lost forever except the embarrassing bits, which are radiated back out over several trillion years in a form that can be decoded only by very patient and deeply unpleasant beings.

This establishment enjoys a unique location: so close to the point of no return that the staff are permanently just about to arrive. The service is, by all accounts, atrocious.

From the diner’s point of view the waiter set off to take the order shortly after the universe began and has been approaching the table ever since at an ever-decreasing rate. The previous compiler had vanished into the index after attempting to cross-reference “infinity” with “a nice sit-down.” The editorial board (a committee that existed in a permanent state of “pending approval”) decided they needed someone who could summarise an entire civilisation in fewer than three pages and still leave room for a joke about towels. I qualified. Barely.

My first assignment arrived as a memo that unfolded itself into a small, officious origami swan and then exploded into text: *Earth. Not demolished. Update entry immediately. Previous description (“Mostly harmless”) now factually incomplete. Do not ask why. We already tried.*

Earth. That damp little world that had somehow survived the bureaucratic equivalent of a hyperspace bypass. This was irregular. Planets scheduled for demolition are expected to have the good grace to stay demolished. It’s considered polite.

I packed my towel (obviously) and set off.

They are a species composed entirely of living stationery—sentient memos, self-replicating carbon paper, and the occasional aggressive stapler. They communicate by collating themselves into increasingly passive-aggressive piles. Their entire civilisation runs on the principle that if a form has not been filled out in triplicate, the event in question has not officially happened.²

A senior Formfillian named Carbon-Copy 7 rustled importantly. “The demolition order for Sol-3 was used as a coaster during the 57th Sub-Committee on Unimportant Rocks. It became slightly damp. Entire star systems have been known to roll there during particularly vigorous vacuuming of the space-time continuum. If that fails, assume the universe is having an off day and make tea. Deeply unhelpful. I made tea anyway. It was terrible.

**Earth**
